These are political assessments of the situation on the ground related to security, political measures that should be taken in order to overcome this, also taking a stand with regard to these matters, a political stand, things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you give the Chamber an idea of the sorts of issues it was dealing with in the months, the few months, leading up to April of 1992?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if we're looking at it on this level, certain incidents were looked into: for example, when the bridge was mined, and also when some other facilities were mined; possibly some ethnic related conflicts, if they did happen, how this was reflected elsewhere. And then also it went beyond that a bit: the situation in Croatia; in Vukovar there was a war; and also some of these units came to Samac, both one and the other, Serb and Croat. Sometimes some people went across. So this was analysed, this situation, it was followed. Then also the mining of some kiosks.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. I have an idea now. Thank you. Can I just ask you if the commission that we have just been talking about maintained any relations with the police and other security organs, or was that done on an ad hoc basis?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was a commission only for the needs of the party, for our political needs.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. You were also asked this morning whether the SDA sent its members to Slavonia for anti-sabotage training --

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honours. To the best of my recollection, the question was not formulated as someone was sent to Slovenia for anti-sabotage training. It was rather different, so perhaps maybe our learned friend could help us during the redirect with some references on the transcript, and then we can follow easily. MR. DI FAZIO: I'll try and assuage Mr. Pantelic's concerns. I don't think I'm misquoting the evidence. May I just very briefly have a look at the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: May I just seek a clarification from you, Mr. Tihic? This is just before April 1992, so the SDA has its commission for security, and I suppose the other two parties also have their commissions and they put up assessments and security reports. So how is the coordination done? I mean, do you have --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: -- different bodies, three different commissions with reports, assessments?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the level of the municipality, there was a council for security and a council for national defence, and that is where the parties brought together their political views and discussed them; that is to say, within the municipality there was a council for security and a council for national defence. And every party considered, within itself, the political situation and the security-related situation, and then it was debated further at municipal level.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tihic. I think Mr. Pantelic's objection was right, but only just. You were, in fact, asked -- the question that was put to you was that the municipal committee of the SDA in Bosanski Samac was involved in sending members for anti-sabotage training in Bosanski Samac, and you said: "Alija Fitozovic was involved in these activities. I knew there were people who were being sent to some kind of training, but that was done by Alija Fitozovic." Now, that's what you said, and I quote from the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I do apologise, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In fact, that was a mistake in transcript. My question was not anti-sabotage, but sabotage units. And then, if you follow the other part of my questioning, I was making a reference to the memoirs of Mr. Tihic, where exactly he said that they were training for sabotage, command, or whatever. It's not anti-sabotage. It's a big difference. So that was my intervention about the transcript, in fact, and then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Oh, I see. MR. DI FAZIO: I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So you have corrected what --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: That is correct. It is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: -- what you wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: This is page 32, and the line 6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Of this morning's proceedings?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Of this morning. And then, in order to clarify that, if you see after this particular question, you will see that I make a reference on exact words of Mr. Tihic. So maybe that's a problem with the translation. But my question was very precise. These were the members, party members, sent to sabotage, command, whatever. Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: I see the reference to "sabotage" alone in later questions and answers, but the record says "anti-sabotage." That's what I read in one of the sentences and in the sentence that I quoted. Now, that isn't going to matter much for my purposes. If there's to be any amendment to the transcript, if Your Honours please, perhaps the interpreters could attend to that and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. The audio people would give us the correct -- what was actually spoken. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. But whether it was "anti-sabotage" or "sabotage" is not what I'm concerned with, so can I please proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right. So you can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: If you allow me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We will get the transcript from the people who listen, and then they will give us the part of the transcript so that everybody can see what was said. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: In fact, Mr. Tihic, later in your evidence, you said you didn't know if it was actually sabotage training, it was just training for defence preparations or something like that. Now, what I'm interested in - and Mr. Pantelic asked you this as well but I don't think you gave a very clear answer - was whether this activity of sending -- of people going to Slavonia for this military training of whatever nature, was conducted under SDA auspices, under SDA approval. Now, was that ever done?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Again, Your Honour, could I have a second, just to check this portion of transcript, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think I catch the problem. Slavonia is the region in Croatia which is just across the river from Samac, and Slavonia was mentioned in context of arming. That's one problem. Probably my friend is mixing, you know, because it's very similar, these terms. And Slovenia is the former republic of Yugoslavia. And my question with regard to Slovenia was whether Mr. Cengic, one of the prominent figures within the SDA party, was involved in armaments from Slovenia to headquarters of SDA in Sarajevo. So we have now three different aspects, actually. So in order to help my friend, I mean, there is not any mention about Slavonia and military training. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All I'm really interested in, Mr. Tihic, is just a simple thing. Did you send -- did the SDA send people off for training outside of Bosnia? That's all I want to know.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The SDA did not send people anywhere to Bosnia or elsewhere, either for sabotage or anti-sabotage training.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. And this activity of Alija Fitozovic for sabotage or anti-sabotage in Slovenia or Slavonia, was it conducted under the auspices of the SDA or was it something that was his own action?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was not done within the SDA, nor was it done by Alija Fitozovic. Anything that had to do with sabotage or anti-sabotage units or training was not done by Alija or the SDA, not in Slavonia, not in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. Okay. You also mentioned today in your evidence in cross-examination that a meeting -- that there was no meeting to set up the TO but that Mato Nujic had, and I quote, "further consultations on this issue." What further consultations were those?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, I said that Mato Nujic talked to us from the SDA and from -- with the HDZ about the establishment of the Territorial Defence headquarters and the names of persons who are supposed to be proposed for that. Whether he talked about this any further with other political parties, I don't know. And that's what I said. Also, I said that no special meeting was held of the municipal assembly or something like that, where this issue was discussed. But Mato Nujic should explain this, whether he talked to someone else, apart from the SDA and the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. You were asked, in the course of your evidence, about plundering and looting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, please, may I have a reference of the page and line so that we can follow on which part of today's transcript my learned colleague is referring so that we can, you know, easy follow that? I mean, because obviously he's making some reference, so would it be fair to know?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I don't think that is the procedure here - we are in re-examination - that counsel has always to cite the page of the transcript. That's not the procedure. MR. DI FAZIO: No, it's not. And I might be able to assist Mr. Pantelic, by coincidence, because I happen to have it here for this morning, but for the other stuff, from the other days, I have not got that and I simply can't do that. So if it's any assistance to Mr. Pantelic in this particular question, I can tell him it's at lines 56 and 57 but I -- with respect, I agree with what the Chamber says. I'm not obliged to point it out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: And it's up to Mr. Pantelic to follow, to remember what the answers were, and things like that, and unless he's challenging that that never arose in cross-examination, that is fine. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Now, you were asked by Mr. Pantelic about plunder and looting on the part of paramilitaries and Her Honour Judge Mumba asked you whether the forces or criminals who loot and plunder do so on their own initiative, so to speak, and Mr. Pantelic adopted that question and posed it to you, and asked you whether these -- such individuals had an individual goal to plunder, and you said yes. Can you rule out any joint intention to plunder?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour, obvious speculating, speculating question. And we are getting beyond the issue of redirect. That's my objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Speculating, yes, I agree. MR. DI FAZIO: But with respect, as my learned colleague points out, Your Honour's question is that whether it was the objective of those who form such forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Forces, yes, to include criminals. MR. DI FAZIO: To include criminals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So that the criminals could go and plunder and do it. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. Now, that part, that aspect of the question, wasn't put by Mr. Pantelic. He merely focused on individuals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, you can ask him. MR. DI FAZIO: I'm asking whether there was a joint -- he can comment on a joint intention on the parts of those particular individuals to plunder and loot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Put it to the witness because what arose there was something like forces, the forces that were formed, the armed forces that were formed, included criminals, right? And those would go and plunder and loot. And I asked whether it was the objective of those people who formed those forces to include criminals for that purpose or were the criminals plundering and looting on their own accord. MR. DI FAZIO: Very well. In that case, Your Honour, I will adopt your question and put it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You heard Her Honour's question, I believe. Was it translated to you?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot claim with certainty what the intention was of those who established these forces when they included criminals in them, whether the intention was, in addition to fighting, to have them plunder as well. However, the rule was, after the fighting, after territories were taken, these forces would loot these territories. It was some kind of a rite of theirs which belonged to them after the successful outcome of the battle.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You were asked about, for want of a better description, the list of traitors. The exhibit is D21/1 ter ID. I don't need to show you that document. I think you recall it from this morning, don't you? It was the list of --

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You said that it originated -- or the effect of your evidence was that it originated somewhere in the SDA. Do you know who the actual author was?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I didn't know, you know. But it was not a big volume that was involved, as far as this leaflet is concerned. It was just typed out. It wasn't in hundreds of copies. Perhaps it was about 10 or 20. But that is not a serious -- it was not done in a serious way.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I'm not suggesting it was. But what I'm interested to know is that -- clarify for the Chamber this, this issue: You say it originated with someone in the SDA. Was it in any way an official document, or did it in any way represent the position of the SDA in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I assumed that it was some of our people from the SDA who did it. And this was not an official stand, you know. It was more of an individual thing, the individual thinking of some people who in that way wanted to provoke, and there was no sign of the SDA there, no letterhead, whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, let's turn to your -- MR. DI FAZIO: I'm sorry. Will the Chamber just bear with me for one moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: Can the witness be provided with D3/ter ID [sic]. D3/2 ID. I'm sorry. Could also the English be placed on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Now, your evidence -- and I am here referring to evidence that you gave in response to Mr. Zecevic's questions on the 6th of November. Your evidence in respect of this document was that you don't recall issuing it; you considered that it was unlikely that you would have done so; that you had no reason to issue Hasan Bicic with such a document; and that you only ever issued one such document, but that was to Jasenica, Fuad.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: -- for the purposes of clarification and fairness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: -- the witness has stated that he gave one document to Jasenica, Fuad and Ibrahim Salkic. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You forgot your -- my learned colleague, you forgot to say "Ibrahim Salkic." You just said "Jasenica, Fuad." MR. DI FAZIO: Oh, I see. I'm sorry. My apologies. That document plainly refers to Ibrahim Salkic as well, the other document. I'm sorry. I wasn't deliberately concealing that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Do you understand, Mr. Tihic, that the other document that I referred to and that I'll be drawing your attention to shortly related not just to Jasenica, Fuad but also to Ibrahim Salkic, okay? Now, let's turn our attention back to this document here, please. Just assuming for the moment that this was a valid document, where would it normally be stored or kept? Assuming for a moment that it was in fact your document, where would it normally have been kept?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the archives of the party.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Was that --

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The protocol in archives.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Would that --

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The office of the party, and that's where it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Yes. I see. And back in the early 1990s, in 1991 and 1992, was it the practice -- tell us, if you can: Was it the practice to use carbon copies or make photocopies? How did you keep records of material that you -- documents that you sent out?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the mechanical machine was used. There were electrical typewriters too, but I think that this was a mechanical one, and it would be typed out in two copies, three copies, a document, depending on how much was necessary, using a carbon, a carbon copy. And then it would be typed out and I would sign, as president. And the party might be given a copy, a carbon copy, and one would remain in the archives.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: As a matter of general practice, back in 1991 and 1992, early part of 1992, did copy documents that you kept in the SDA, copy documents that you signed - I'm not referring to the original that was used or sent to someone, but the copy document that was kept in the SDA and that you signed - would they have had your signature on them, either copy signature or original?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There had to be a signature on the copy, not on the stamp; not stamp, but copy -- but signature, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. I've done with that document. May the witness now be shown D9 -- it's now D9 -- Exhibit D9/2, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic asked you questions about this document on Wednesday morning, and you said that you recall the episode that the document referred to but that you weren't certain about the authenticity of this particular document, and you commented that the document had no logo, no letterhead, was unsigned, didn't say "president" at the bottom. My question is: Can you explain the absence of those features from this document?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see that this document has a protocol number either. I don't know if this is the logo type of the machine or not, whether it was different from the previous one. I said that I cannot assert, confirm, the authenticity of the document. I would rather say it was not, but I don't know. But I did say that I told my secretary to write a document to this effect and to bring it to me to sign. This isn't signed. It wouldn't say "Municipal Board Bosanski Samac." It would say "president" first. Then there would be "Sulejman Tihic," my name, and I would sign it. So I don't know how come we have a certificate like this one here. But as to the contents, yes, I did agree to have my secretary write a piece of paper to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. I now want to ask you some questions about the actual episode that D9 purports to refer to, okay, the actual factual matters relating to Mr. Fuad and Mr. Ibrahim and the acquiring and receipt of equipment. In your evidence, you said that Ibrahim Salkic was a member of the SDA. Can I ask you this? Are you aware of Ibrahim Salkic ever having left the SDA?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. Why did Mr. Jasenica, Fuad, approach you with the sort of proposal that you discussed? And I'm referring of course to the going to Croatia for the purposes of acquiring weapons.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Jasenica contacted me because we are distant cousins, and he said that he had some people in Croatia, as far as I remember, who would be able to give him weapons, but that he needed a certificate of some kind to support his request. But I didn't believe he'd do that. I didn't believe he'd actually go ahead with it, because he was a man who liked to exaggerate and to make himself look more important than he was. So I never thought that anything would come of that, of that certificate, and all of rest of it. But later on, he told me that he didn't actually hand over the certificate, that he didn't need to, and that they gave it to him even without the certificate. At the time, judging by the date, if it was the 14th, if the date is correct here, then the staff had just been formed that day or perhaps the day before.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe that's why he came to me, because he didn't know of the existence of the TO staff and headquarters, that they had actually been established.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic asked you questions about Mr. Jasenica, and then asked you, "Mr. Tihic, what kind of equipment are we talking about here?" And you answered, "Well, the two of them, or one of them, I think Fuad came and said he had a connection of some kind in Croatia and said that he could procure some weapons, that he would need a certificate to prove that he was there on behalf of someone." In your answer, you started to say that the two of them approached you and then you said, "or one of them," and then you said you think it was Fuad. Can you say with any degree of certainty whether or not Ibrahim Salkic approached you as well? That's what I want to know. I'm only talking about the approach. I'm not talking about the whole episode. I'm only talking about the approach. Do you want me to reread your answer?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I know what you're asking me, but I can't remember whether Ibrahim came to me or whether it was just Fuad Jasenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. You then went on to describe the result of their venture and you said - and this is part of the same answer - and I quote, "And not much time went by, perhaps a day or two, and I received information that they had brought in, I think, 50 automatic rifles, and I told them to take them off to the Territorial Defence headquarters in Bosanski Samac, which had been set up two or three days prior to that. So that those weapons were taken there straight away, and I assume that they were distributed later on in part or at least." What I want to know is this: Did you actually see Fuad and/or Ibrahim Salkic at the time of the arrival of the weapons in Bosanski Samac, or did you simply issue instructions as to what was to be done with the weapons?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think Fuad came to my office and said -- I asked him, "Where is it?" And he showed me -- pointed out a kombi van and he said, "Over there." The van was over by the embankment. And I said, "Take it to the Territorial Defence headquarters and hand it over there." He did that -- sorry, he did that, and I know that it was issued -- later on the weapons were issued to members of the Territorial Defence. I think that when Samac was attacked, some of the weapons stayed on in the warehouse.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Can you say with any degree of certainty if Ibrahim Salkic was present on this occasion when you issued instructions to Fuad as to what he should do with the weapons? If you can't say so, please let us know.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Krgovic asked you some questions on the 7th of November, also in the morning, and he asked you about Mr. Miroslav Tadic, and asked you about the episode where you saw him in the TO. You gave evidence that he was there for about five minutes. In that time, would he have been able to see the condition of the men who were in, inside the TO?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was the first or the second day, because later on, I was transferred to the SUP building, to the prison in the police station. Now, whether he could have seen or not, at that particular moment, well, there weren't that many people who were beaten on that first or second day. People looked not too bad, if I can put it that way. Some had been beaten but not that badly yet. So whether he did see them, he could have seen them, but as I say, there were not that many people. Had he come on day ten, we were all -- they were all black and blue, everybody had injuries. But on the first and second day, there were fewer people, and fewer people who were injured and bruised. If he came across them, he could have seen them. If he went the other way around, he might not have seen them. So I can't really say. But had he come ten days later, everyone had visible injuries.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. You described an episode involving a gentleman named Senad Memic and the transportation of weapons on behalf of the SDA. This episode involved a truck breaking down in Bosanski Samac and the taking of 20 rifles. Where were those weapons destined for?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he was driving weapons with a truck with Ljubljana [Realtime transcript read in error "Lubana"] number plates, and then they transferred it to the van belonging to the veterinary station, and then as remuneration, he gave them a box with 20 rifles, and those rifles were given there, but he distributed them among our guards and things like that, the watches that we kept and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Madam President, in the interest of justice maybe it would be good to see this Ljubljana plates were from which state maybe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: To do what?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Maybe we could hear from which state Ljubljana plates are belonging, simply as that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Oh, I see, the plates on the motor vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Plates on the truck, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Region or state, thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: Would Your Honour just bear with me for a moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO: I thought I had my geography wrong but Ljubljana is the capital of Slovenia, unless I'm wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Is that so?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, because in transcript it's "Lubana," which is a little bit unclear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Oh, it's the spelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Spelling. It's not Lubana. It is L-j-u-b-l-j-a-n-a. MR. DI FAZIO: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: It's not Lubana. It's Slovenia, of course. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: These were Slovenian plates, were they?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. And yes, thank you. Mr. Lazarevic asked you a number of questions about the 4th Detachment. And he asked you if the arming of the 4th Detachment was a public exercise. You said that arms were distributed to members of the 4th Detachment, they took their weapons in their cars to the homes of other members of the 4th Detachment. In your experience, in the former Yugoslavia, was it the practice for army soldiers to take their weapons home?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, as a matter of clarification, as I remember, Mr. Tihic stated that the weaponry was delivered in the facilities of Mladost, if I remember correctly, of Samac industry of textile, actually, that it was delivered there to the members of the 4th Detachment, and also delivered in the houses of the members. Just a matter of clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I was wondering what the difference was. MR. DI FAZIO: All I'm interested in is the use -- the keeping of weapons at home by members of the 4th Detachment. How the weapons originally came into Bosanski Samac is not my concern. My concern is the fact that 4th Detachment members, members of the JNA, taking their guns home, keeping them with them. That doesn't seem to me to be soldierly practice. Now, I just want to know if that was the case --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. And in any case, Mr. Lazarevic has cleared what he wasn't sure about, so -- MR. DI FAZIO: I'm not trying to misquote the evidence, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: You can proceed. MR. DI FAZIO: -- that's not what I'm interested in at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Mr. Tihic, you may have had that exchange translated to you. You understand my question. What I want to know is this: In the former Yugoslavia, did soldiers take their guns home, keep them at home? I'm not talking about officers or generals; I'm talking about the usual soldiers.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, no. Only at the military training sessions. And when they came back, they would leave it at the headquarters. They wouldn't take them home. No, you wouldn't take weapons home.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. You were also being asked questions by Mr. Lazarevic in relation to the 4th Detachment, and you were asked -- yes. You were asked whether it was by order of the commander of the 17th Tactical Group that the 4th Detachment was formed, and you said, "I think it was precisely through that order. However, we thought that was illegal because this is a form of Territorial Defence." And counsel then said, "You have already presented your point of view while giving testimony." I want to hear what your point of view was on the illegality of the 4th Detachment. What were you about to say at that point?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We consider that this form of organisation of the JNA was not in conformity with the law and that units of that kind can only exist within the frameworks of the Territorial Defence and at no events within the JNA. The Yugoslav People's Army and their units, and its units, imply the existence of barracks, uniforms, and life and work organised in the barracks, whereas units in the field, people sitting in their homes and going about their daily business, that can only be the Territorial Defence. And that's why we consider that the JNA came under the competence of the Territorial Defence and that it was an illegal act to form the 4th Detachment and the other similar ones. That was our opinion. That's what we said to Lieutenant Colonel Nikolic at the National Defence Council, that he had no authority to set up units of that kind, according to the law, because units of that kind could only exist within the Territorial Defence and not within the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lazarevic also asked you about the meeting in Prud where discussion of a joint HDZ and SDA crisis staff occurred. You gave evidence that that meeting did not produce any agreement for a crisis staff, for such a crisis staff, and that you took a strong stance against it. He then asked you about a second meeting at a place called - and I'm not sure of the pronunciation. It's either Grebnice or Grebnica - I'm not sure, where the same subject was discussed.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't catch the witness' remark.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't hear what the witness said. Can the witness repeat what he said? MR. DI FAZIO: I think the witness was giving the proper, correct pronunciation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Of what? MR. DI FAZIO: Of Grebnice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Proceed. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Now, the same subject was discussed, but you weren't asked whether at that second meeting any agreement was reached on a joint HDZ or SDA crisis staff, and that's what I want to know. What was the result of the second meeting?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't attend that second meeting, but a joint crisis staff was not set up.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I have already touched upon this issue earlier in this re-examination, but Mr. Lazarevic also touched on the issue, and that is, namely, the proposal endorsing Bozanovic and Alija Fitozovic as TO leaders, and that proposal being sent to Sarajevo. In your evidence, and in answer to questions by Mr. Lazarevic, you said that that procedure that you adopted was the correct procedure but that no meeting was ever held to discuss those proposed appointments with the Municipal Assembly. My question is this: Was there ever time for a meeting to be held before the hostilities began and for the Municipal Assembly to consider that very issue?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Had they been in agreement, they would have found the time, and Mato Nujic probably thought that there wouldn't be agreement. So perhaps because of that, he didn't convene the meeting, realistically speaking. Because the ratio of forces was roughly 50/50, it was difficult to take a decision. And Mato made use of his right to propose that, but, at the same time, responsibility if he had made a mistake, doing it without the Municipal Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. You were also asked this question and this answer, and I need to quote it, and I'd ask that you listen carefully to the question in particular:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Can we agree that members of the 4th Detachment took the right banks of the Sava and Bosna rivers, respectively, in order to prevent the HVO from penetrating?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, yes, and on the bridge on the Drina and on the Bosna. So in that question there were two questions: First of all, whether the 4th Detachment took the right banks of the Sava and Bosna River.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. My learned colleague has just mentioned river Drina, and it has nothing to do with Samac. I mean, it's river Sava, I believe. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. I'm grateful to my learned friend. It's not a matter that's going to be of particular significance. If there's a -- I've got "Drina" here in my transcript. I see it here: D-r-i-n-a. But whether it's Sava or Drina matters not for my purposes, and I'm sure it won't trouble Mr. Lazarevic when he hears my question asked in full. Because I'm not interested in what the names of the rivers are. It's the two-barrelled question that I'm interested in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. I think his concern was that one river is in another region and the other one is in a totally different area, I think. Yes. So he needed to have that corrected. So he has corrected it himself. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. Well, perhaps I'll put in "Sava," the word "Sava," substitute the word "Sava."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. After that, I just want to go back and I want you to understand the question clearly. I'll just quickly read it for you again.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Can we agree that members of the 4th Detachment took the right banks of the Sava and Bosna rivers, respectively, in order to prevent the HVO from penetrating?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, yes, and the bridge on the Sava, on the Bosna. Now, there are two questions there. One, did they take those banks; and two, was it to prevent the HVO from penetrating? You seem to agree with the proposition. I want to know your answer to both aspects of the question, and in particular, whether it was to prevent the HVO from penetrating.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, members of the 4th Detachment took -- assumed positions on the right bank of the Bosna, on the embankment that was by the river. I don't know about the Sava. I don't know them taking up positions on the Sava bank. Now, why they had done that, I said probably to prevent reinforcements from coming in to town from the village of Prud and the HVO and the rest. Probably because of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: The re-examination isn't complete, but my colleague, Ms. Reidy --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Is continuing with Ms. Reidy, yes. MR. DI FAZIO: -- has a few questions on another aspect of Mr. Pantelic's questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Mr. Tihic, my question, or series of short questions, just goes around one part of Mr. Pantelic's examination in cross.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And while I don't want to set a precedent, Mr. Pantelic, in case you want to follow me closely, it's on page either 3753 to 3754 of the official transcript or pages 124 to 128 of yesterday's, depending on which numbering system you're using.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And what that questioning was about was about whether or not the central government in Bosnia-Herzegovina controlled all the territory. And you had answered that it could not control the entire territory because the Yugoslav People's Army did not allow them to do that as well as various paramilitary formations, et cetera. You were then asked to point out on the map, which for the record is Prosecution Exhibit P15, which areas were under the control of the central government, et cetera. And Mr. Pantelic concluded that part of his statement by saying, "Let the record show that the witness explained on the Exhibit P15 the regions under the control of the central government of Bosnia and Herzegovina in the period from mid-April 1992 and the other years." Now what I want to clarify is in fact, while you did indicate a lot of areas, Mr. Pantelic never at any time tied down the time period which went hand in hand with the areas that were controlled. So I understand you began by pointing out the areas which were under the control of the central government in April 1992. Can you tell me whether there was a significant change in the area in May 1992?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were changes in May and the month of June and later, throughout the war, there were certain changes. But the central government controlled central Bosnia, Tuzla, the Tuzla canton, so to speak, down towards Mostar and Mostar, Krajina, Bihac, and that area of the Bihac Krajina, actually. They kept that under their control all the time. That didn't change. As for the other towns, it depended on when they would fall. Some fell in April, some fell -- I don't know. Let's take Srebrenica, that was 1995. It was lost from under their control. And Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: My question --

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And then later the territory was enlarged again and Sanski Most was liberated, and Kljuc was liberated and then Donja Vakuf was liberated.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: On the basis of that, can you say was there a dramatic increase in the control of the territory enjoyed by the central government of Bosnia-Herzegovina between 6th of April, 1992, and the 23rd of May, 1992? Or if not, is there even a decrease in the amount of territory that the government controlled?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The territory was decreased between the 6th of April and the 23rd of May, the territory under the control of --

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And just my last question again, between May and, say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The answer was not completed.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I apologise, I didn't hear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I didn't hear the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness broke off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, the witness, I think, broke off. Can the answer be completed, please? The answer was, "The territory was decreased between 6th of April and the 23rd of May, the territory under the control of -- " Can the answer be completed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The territory under the control of the central government was decreased, and the central authorities of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. Sorry, I didn't realise I was interrupting you. Then my last question would be, again, between May 23rd and, say, the beginning of 1993, was there again a dramatic increase in the effective control enjoyed by the central government, in terms of the amount of territory?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Obviously leading, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Obviously leading question, so please let my learned colleague rephrase that.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: With respect, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: The witness should give his answer to the best of his knowledge and without this kind of question. Maybe it's appropriate for cross but not for redirect. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I don't appreciate, because this is re-examination. Anyway, Ms. Reidy, you can do your best to satisfy Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Mr. Tihic, between May -- the 23rd of May, 1992, and let's take the beginning of 1993, can you say whether there was any change, increase or decrease, in the territory which the central government of Bosnia-Herzegovina enjoyed?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that until the end of 1992, there was a small decrease in the territory.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That's the end of my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Is that the end of re-examination? MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, it is, if Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: Mr. Tihic, I just want to get a clearer picture on the Territorial Defence. Now, before the formation of the 4th Detachment, can you please tell us very briefly what was the framework and the extent of the framework for Territorial Defence in Bosnia-Herzegovina and particularly in your area, and who participated in it?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Territorial Defence is a constitutional category of the constitution of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and of the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It is also a legal category. That is the legal framework. All the nationalities of Bosnia-Herzegovina took part in it: Serbs, Croats, Bosniaks and others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: Now, the next thing you said was that the 4th Detachment can only exist within the framework of the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: So in 1992, the 4th Detachment was formed through the 17th Tactical Command?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: So what does that mean? Were they trying to replace Territorial Defence through Territorial Defence units?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, the Territorial Defence was under the control of the presidency of the -- of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That is to say, that it was headed by Alija Izetbegovic. The JNA was under the control of the General Staff, Slobodan Milosevic, and that team from Belgrade. It did not suit them to have Territorial Defence units established, you see, so the JNA established something that it was not in charge of. It established a unit that did not belong to it, that had to be within the command of the Territorial Defence and the presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That was the reason why they established this, you see, because they did not want this to be under the control of the presidency -- the command of the presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina but under the control of the General Staff of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: So did the Territorial Defence units at the end become ineffective?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In view of the fact that weapons were taken away from the Territorial Defence, that the JNA took weapons, they became inefficient or how shall we -- ineffective in Bosanski Samac, and in other places.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Out of the answers from the questions from the Bench, any clarification? The Prosecution? MR. DI FAZIO: No, no, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, on behalf of all defence team, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tihic, for giving evidence to the Trial Chamber. You are now released. You can go.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In the meantime, Your Honours, could we follow the practice of the swap of the position of the defendants because there is a new witness coming?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Before the witness comes, all right, yes. What would you suggest?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Let the Registrar give a proposition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I thought you would like to say which seats.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I don't have any particular -- let's be quick. Maybe Mr. Zaric can come here and Mr. Blagoje Simic can go to the other place so that we don't waste so much time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, we can proceed. The Prosecution -- I hope the usher is coming with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Before the witness arrives, can we go into private session for one minute?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Oh, yes. Can we go into private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The Defence counsel, I take it, since we shall proceed tomorrow morning, you would like the setup of the accused to be the same tomorrow morning as it is now?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that is correct. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right. The witness can be brought in.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you, please sit down. Yes, Mr. Weiner, you can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Would you please introduce yourself to the Court?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC
utterances.text: I am Esad Dagovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us how old you are?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Thirty-three.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What's your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC
utterances.text: The 28th of May, 1969.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Are you married?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Do you have any children?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: How many?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC
utterances.text: One, seven months old.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Boy, girl?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Girl.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Where were you born?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC
utterances.text: In Gradacac.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And are you a member of any ethnic group, sir?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC
utterances.text: I'm a Bosniak Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Where did you go to school?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC
utterances.text: In Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What did you study?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC
utterances.text: In Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And what did you study there, in high school?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to correct you. It was a vocational secondary school for electrotechnical engineering.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. April of 1992, could you tell us where you were living?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC
utterances.text: I lived in Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: How long had you lived in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC
utterances.text: From when I was born.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you have any other family members that were living with you in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Who is that?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC
utterances.text: My mother, my father and my brother.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please speak into the microphone?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Maybe he should be helped to get closer to the microphones.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, were you a member of any political party?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was a member of the SDA.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were you an active member?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC
utterances.text: An active member? Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Did you own any weapons?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What did you own?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC
utterances.text: I owned a pistol, Crvena Zastava 9 millimetres, and I had a permit for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Where did you get that permit?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC
utterances.text: I got it from the Ministry of the Interior in Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, where did you work?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC
utterances.text: I worked at the pizzeria called Rendezvous in Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What did you do there?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC
utterances.text: I was a waiter.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And how long had you worked there?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC
utterances.text: About three or four years.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Do you know who owned that pizzeria?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Who?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Hasan Bicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did any of the other Bicics work there?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, his brother, Muhamed Bicic worked there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And what was your relationship with the Bicics?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC
utterances.text: We had an excellent relationship. We were like brothers; perhaps I should put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And how was the Bicic family viewed or considered in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they were a well-respected family of means.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, you talked about their families being of means. Could you describe the means of your family, the wealth of your family, prior to April 18th, 1992?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you. My family was relatively a middle-class family, but my grandfather was a Beg. "Beg" is a title among Bosnian Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And what is a Beg? Could you please describe it to the Court.

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Beg was a title among the Bosnian Muslims. It meant that -- along with it went a large portion of property. He had a lot of shops, real estate, both houses and arable land.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: How long had your family lived in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC
utterances.text: My family lived in Samac from its very inception, that is to say, after they were expelled from Uzice in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, did you own any homes? Did you and your family own any homes in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: How many?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC
utterances.text: We owned my father's house and we owned my grandmother's house, that is to say, my father's mother's house; namely, two houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And where were they in relation to each other? Where were they located?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC
utterances.text: In the street of Pere Bosica, that is to say, in the centre of town.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And were the two houses near each other?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They were within the same courtyard.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you own any vehicles or have any vehicles?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And could you tell the Court what you had?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC
utterances.text: I had a Ford Capri, and I used a vehicle that was given to me by Hasan Bicic. That was a Suzuki Jeep. How should I put it? I had it with me all the time, except that it was not owned by me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And where did you store that Jeep?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC
utterances.text: I kept it in my yard, or sometimes in a garage that Hasan Bicic had near his house.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And sir, where did you and your family members store their money? Did you use banks or did you keep the money at home?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC
utterances.text: In view of the poor situation of our banks and the prevailing insecurity, we did not keep money in the bank; we kept money at home. We did have a bank account, though, but there was very little money in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, having lived your whole life in Bosanski Samac, or up to 1992 your whole life in Bosanski Samac, I'm going to ask you if you know certain people. Do you know a man by the name of Simo Zaric?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'd ask you to look around the courtroom, and could you tell me if he is in this courtroom at this time?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The gentleman is over here, at that first table, and he has grey hair and a chequered suit.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Do you know a man by the name of Milan Simic?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Can you tell if he's in this courtroom at this time?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He's the first sitting on the left-hand side, in a blue jacket.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Do you know a man by the name of Miroslav Tadic?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Can you see him in the courtroom at this time?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He's sitting in the middle.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And do you know a man by the name of Blagoje Simic?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And can you tell the Court whether he's sitting in this courtroom at this time?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he is. He is sitting on the right-hand side. He's the man with the beard.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honours, may the record reflect that all four defendants have been identified by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to go to April 16th, the evening of April 16th, the evening just before the attack. Could you tell us whether you were working on that evening?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Where were you working?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC
utterances.text: At the pizzeria.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And could you tell us what sort of crowd you had on that night.

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Since I was used to seeing customers of all ethnicities, that night I did not see any clients of Serb ethnicity, and that is to say that there were very few customers in the pizzeria, generally speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: As a result of the very small number of patrons, did you do anything? Did you close early? Did you -- what did you do?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Normal working hours were until 12.00 or perhaps until 1.00 at night; however, that night I closed at 11.00 in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: After you closed, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC
utterances.text: After I closed the pizzeria, I went home. Since it was too early for me to go to bed, I watched a movie.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sometime around 2.00, 3.00 in the morning, did something happen?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I heard shooting in town.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What did you do?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC
utterances.text: What did I do? I waited for a while and then I went out into the yard, or rather, in front of my house, into the street, to see what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And while you were outside, did you see anything?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What did you see?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC
utterances.text: I saw military vehicles that were moving in all directions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What did you do next?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Nothing. I went back into the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Later that morning, did you go anywhere?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Where did you go?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC
utterances.text: I went to the owner of the pizzeria in order to hand him in the money earned the previous day.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And who was that, the owner?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC
utterances.text: The owner was, as I had previously said, Hasan Bicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And did you go to the Bicic home?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And where was the Bicic home in relation to your home?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC
utterances.text: It was halfway from my house to the pizzeria, that is to say, 50 metres away from my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: After you gave the Bicics the money, did you return home?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And did you see the Bicics again later that morning?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: How did you come to see them?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Since their mother and the wives of Hasan and Muhamed Bicic, they came to my mother's for breakfast and coffee.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: After you had breakfast, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC
utterances.text: After breakfast, since there was shooting in town, we decided, my father and my brother and I, to clean up the basement a bit, and also to put bricks on the windows so that we would have a shelter in case there was shelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Pardon me. Your Honours, since it's 5.00, would you like to break at this moment, or should I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We will adjourn and resume our proceedings tomorrow morning at 0930 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 9th day of November, 2001, at 9.30 a.m. 24 25
